guide.summary: This unit develops rotational kinematics and Newton's second law for rotation: angular quantities, torque as a cross product, rotational inertia (including integrals and the parallel-axis theorem), static equilibrium, and systems combining rotation and translation (pulleys with mass).

sections.heading: Rotational kinematics
sections.body: Angular position θ, angular velocity ω = dθ/dt, and angular acceleration α = dω/dt follow the same calculus relationships as linear motion; with constant α, the rotational kinematic equations apply. Linear and angular quantities for a point at radius r: s = rθ, v = rω, a_tangential = rα, a_centripetal = ω²r.

sections.heading: Torque and rotational inertia
sections.body: Torque τ = r × F, with magnitude rF sin θ (equivalently, force times lever arm). Newton's second law for rotation: Στ = Iα about a fixed axis or the center of mass. Rotational inertia I = Σmr² or ∫r² dm depends on mass distribution relative to the axis. Common results: thin rod about center ML²/12, about end ML²/3; solid disk/cylinder ½MR²; hoop MR²; solid sphere (2/5)MR². Parallel-axis theorem: I = I_cm + Md². To derive I by integration, write dm = λ dx (rod) and integrate r² dm over the object.

sections.heading: Equilibrium and connected systems
sections.body: Static equilibrium requires ΣF = 0 and Στ = 0 about any point; choose the pivot to eliminate unknown forces. For a pulley with mass, the tension differs on each side: (T₂ − T₁)R = Iα, with a = αR if the string doesn't slip. For an Atwood machine with a disk pulley of mass M: a = (m₂ − m₁)g/(m₁ + m₂ + M/2). A rod pivoted at one end and released from horizontal has α = 3g/2L initially, so its free end accelerates at 3g/2, faster than free fall.

sections.heading: Worked example: rotational inertia by integration
sections.body: For a thin rod of mass M and length L rotating about one end, I = ∫r² dm = ∫₀ᴸ x²(M/L) dx = ML²/3. About its center, I = ML²/12. The parallel-axis theorem connects them: I_end = I_cm + M(L/2)² = ML²/12 + ML²/4 = ML²/3. Rotational inertia depends on how mass is distributed relative to the axis.

sections.heading: Worked example: a pulley with mass
sections.body: A 2.0 kg block hangs from a rope wrapped around a solid disk pulley (mass 4.0 kg, radius 0.10 m). For the block, mg − T = ma. For the pulley, TR = Iα = (½MR²)(a/R), so T = ½Ma = 2.0a. Combining, (2.0)(9.8) = (2.0 + 2.0)a, so a = 4.9 m/s² and T = 9.8 N. The massive pulley reduces the block's acceleration compared with a massless pulley.

sections.heading: Worked example: static equilibrium
sections.body: A uniform 4.0 m beam of weight 200 N is supported by a hinge at the wall and a cable at the far end making 30° with the beam. Taking torques about the hinge: T sin 30° × 4.0 = 200 × 2.0, so T = 200 N. Then horizontal and vertical force balance give the hinge forces.

sections.heading: Common errors
sections.body: Students forget the lever arm's perpendicular component, mix up torque directions, and use the wrong rotational inertia formula.

sections.heading: Exam connection
sections.body: Questions ask you to derive rotational inertia, analyze connected systems with pulleys, and solve equilibrium problems with ladders and beams.

sections.heading: Laboratory and experimental design
sections.body: To measure rotational inertia, wrap a string around a rotating platform's axle, attach a hanging mass, and measure the mass's acceleration. Using τ = Iα and the relation a = αr, calculate I. Graphs of applied torque versus angular acceleration have slope I.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body: θ, ω = dθ/dt, α = dω/dt; τ = r × F = rF sin θ; Στ = Iα; I = Σmr² = ∫r² dm; I = I_cm + Md²; v = ωr, a_t = αr.

sections.heading: Derivation tips
sections.body: When deriving rotational results, choose the axis carefully, write torque equations with signs for direction, and connect linear and angular quantities with a = αr when strings do not slip. Use the parallel-axis theorem instead of re-integrating when the axis is shifted.

sections.heading: Graph skills
sections.body: On an angular velocity-versus-time graph, the slope gives angular acceleration and the area gives angular displacement. A graph of torque versus angular acceleration is linear with slope equal to rotational inertia.

keyTakeaways: τ = rF sin θ; Στ = Iα.
Mass farther from axis → larger I → smaller α.
commonMistakes: Using the wrong rotational inertia for the axis (forgetting parallel-axis theorem).
Assuming tension is equal on both sides of a massive pulley.
Measuring the lever arm along the force rather than perpendicular to it.
Mixing degrees and radians in rotational kinematics.
Forgetting that pivot forces can be nonzero even when they produce no torque.
examTips: Derive I with an integral when the object is unusual (variable density).
Write separate Newton's law equations for each hanging mass and the pulley.
For equilibrium, place the pivot where the unknown force acts.
Use a_cm = αr_cm to find pivot forces.
guide.cramSheet:
**Kinematics:** ω = dθ/dt · α = dω/dt · v = rω · a_t = rα · a_c = ω²r

**Torque:** τ = rF sin θ · Στ = Iα

**I:** ∫r² dm · rod center ML²/12 · rod end ML²/3 · disk ½MR² · hoop MR² · sphere (2/5)MR² · I = I_cm + Md²

**Equilibrium:** ΣF = 0, Στ = 0

**Massive pulley:** a = (m₂ − m₁)g/(m₁ + m₂ + I/R²)

vocab.definition: The rate of change of angular position, ω = dθ/dt.
The rate of change of angular velocity, α = dω/dt.
The rotational effect of a force: τ = r × F.
The perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of action of a force.
Resistance to angular acceleration: I = ∫r² dm.
I = I_cm + Md² for an axis parallel to one through the center of mass.
A state with zero net force and zero net torque.
Linear acceleration along the path: a_t = rα.
Acceleration toward the axis: a_c = ω²r.
The angle subtended by an arc equal to the radius; required in rotational equations.
An object whose shape doesn't change as it rotates.
The force exerted by an axle or hinge on a rotating object.

choices.text: The hoop, because all its mass is at the maximum radius

choices.text: The tension on the 2.0 kg side is greater.
The tension on the 4.0 kg side is greater than on the 2.0 kg side.

practice.explanation: T₂ = 4(9.8 − 2.8) = 28 N; T₁ = 2(9.8 + 2.8) = 25.2 N. The difference provides the torque to accelerate the pulley.

practice.explanation: Torques about left end: F_R(6) = 400(3) + 600(2) = 2,400 → F_R = 400 N.

choices.text: The floor's friction force equals the wall's normal force in magnitude.
No friction is needed because the wall is frictionless.

practice.topic: Newton's Second Law in Rotational Form
practice.prompt: A thin uniform rod of mass M and length L is pivoted about a frictionless axle at one end. It is held horizontal and released from rest.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Starting from the definition of rotational inertia, derive the rod's rotational inertia about the pivot.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Derive the rod's angular acceleration immediately after release.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Determine the linear acceleration of the free end immediately after release, and compare it to g.

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Determine the magnitude and direction of the force exerted by the pivot on the rod immediately after release.

parts.label: E
parts.prompt: A student says nothing can fall faster than g. Explain why the free end's acceleration doesn't violate any physical law.

rubric.description: I = ∫r² dm with dm = (M/L) dx, from 0 to L.
τ = Mg(L/2), weight acting at the center of mass.
a_cm = α(L/2) = 3g/4 downward; Mg − F_p = M(3g/4).
The end is not in free fall; it's part of a rigid body rotating about a pivot.
The rod's internal forces push the far end along while the center of mass accelerates at only 3g/4 < g; the pivot supports part of the weight.

practice.sampleResponse:
A. I = ∫r² dm. For a uniform rod, dm = (M/L) dx, with x from 0 to L measured from the pivot: I = (M/L)∫₀^L x² dx = (M/L)(L³/3) = ML²/3.

B. The weight acts at the center of mass, a distance L/2 from the pivot and perpendicular to the horizontal rod: τ = MgL/2. Στ = Iα → α = (MgL/2)/(ML²/3) = 3g/(2L).

C. a_end = αL = (3g/2L)(L) = 3g/2, which is greater than g.

D. The center of mass accelerates downward at a_cm = α(L/2) = 3g/4. Newton's second law for the rod (down positive): Mg − F_p = M(3g/4), so F_p = Mg/4, directed upward.

E. The free end isn't a freely falling object; it's part of a rigid rod rotating about a fixed pivot. The rod's center of mass accelerates at only 3g/4, less than g, because the pivot pushes up. Internal forces in the rigid rod drive the outer end faster than the center, so the far end's acceleration can exceed g without violating Newton's laws.
